questions.stem: How is mean arterial pressure calculated?
questions.why: MAP equals the diastolic pressure plus one third of the difference between systolic and diastolic. A pressure of 120/60 gives 60 plus 20, or 80.

options.t: The systolic and diastolic pressures simply averaged
options.why: A straight average overweights systole relative to the time spent in it.

options.t: Systolic minus a third of the pulse pressure, in mmHg
options.why: The formula builds up from the diastolic, because the heart spends most of its cycle there.

options.t: Cardiac output multiplied by the heart rate
options.why: Cardiac output times systemic vascular resistance gives blood pressure, not MAP.

options.t: Diastolic plus a third of the pulse pressure

questions.stem: Which two relationships does the lecture use to connect the heart to blood pressure?
questions.why: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume, and blood pressure is cardiac output times systemic vascular resistance. Every shock state is a failure somewhere in that chain.

options.t: CO equals HR times SVR; BP equals CO times SV
options.why: That swaps stroke volume and resistance between the two equations.

options.t: CO equals MAP times HR; BP equals CO times SV
options.why: MAP is a result of these relationships rather than an input to them.

options.t: CO equals HR times SV; BP equals CO times SVR
CO equals SV divided by HR; BP equals CO plus SVR
options.why: Cardiac output is a product of rate and stroke volume, not a quotient.

questions.stem: What are the three components of the perfusion triangle?
questions.why: A pump to move it, fluid to move, and a container to move it through. Every category of shock fails one of the three, and the failure tells you what to give.

options.why: Those describe how the pump performs, only one side of the triangle.
Those are what perfusion delivers, not the parts of the system.

options.t: The pump, the fluid, and the container
The heart, the lungs, and the kidneys
options.why: Those are organs affected by shock rather than the components of the model.

questions.stem: At what systolic pressure do the baroreceptors begin to fire in response to hypovolemia?
questions.why: Baroreceptor stimulation kicks in around a systolic of 60 to 80. That is late — the patient has already been compensating through other mechanisms well before the pressure fell that far.

options.why: That range is normal and does not trigger a baroreceptor response.
By that pressure compensation is already well under way and failing.
Compensation begins later than that in this lecture's account.

questions.stem: Which classes of hemorrhagic shock are compensated, and which are decompensated?
questions.why: Classes I and II are compensated — the body is holding the pressure up. Classes III and IV are decompensated. Decompensation corresponds to losing more than 30 percent of blood volume.

options.t: I compensated; II, III and IV decompensated
options.why: Class II is still a compensated state.

options.t: I and II compensated; III and IV decompensated
All four are compensated until the pressure falls
options.why: Blood pressure is a late sign, which is why classes are not defined by it alone.

options.t: I, II and III compensated; IV decompensated
options.why: Class III has already decompensated.

questions.stem: What percentage of blood volume loss marks decompensated shock?
questions.why: Past 30 percent the compensatory mechanisms can no longer hold the pressure. That is where the blood pressure finally drops — and why a normal pressure never rules out significant loss.

options.why: 15 percent is the boundary of class I, still fully compensated.
A ten percent loss is often asymptomatic in a healthy adult.
By 50 percent the patient is well beyond the point of decompensation.

questions.stem: What does the lecture call the best indication of tissue perfusion?
questions.why: The brain is the least tolerant organ of poor perfusion, so mental status changes before the numbers do. A confused or combative patient with a normal blood pressure is a perfusion problem until proven otherwise.

options.why: Blood pressure is maintained by compensation until late, so it lags behind perfusion.
Rate rises for many reasons and does not directly report perfusion.
Refill is useful but is affected by temperature and age.

questions.stem: What mortality does the lecture attribute to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome?
questions.why: 60 to 90 percent. It is the endpoint of prolonged poor perfusion, which is the argument for treating shock before the pressure falls rather than after.

options.why: That understates the mortality given.
MODS carries a far higher mortality than that.
The figure given leaves a meaningful survival range.

questions.stem: What scene time does the lecture set for the critical patient?
questions.why: Ten minutes. Almost nothing that fixes a critical patient happens on scene, so time there is time not spent moving toward the thing that does.

options.why: Tighter than the standard taught, and rarely achievable.
Twice the target given.
The point of the target is that definitive care is elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which vasopressor does the lecture pair with warm septic shock, and which with cold?
questions.why: Warm shock is vasodilated, so norepinephrine's stronger alpha effect tightens the container. Cold shock needs the pump driven, so epinephrine's greater beta-1 effect is the better fit.

options.t: Dopamine for warm shock and norepinephrine for cold shock
options.why: Dopamine is the cardiogenic-shock agent in this lecture.

options.t: Norepinephrine for both presentations, at different doses
options.why: The two presentations call for different receptor profiles, not different doses.

options.t: Epinephrine for warm shock and norepinephrine for cold shock
options.why: That reverses the two.

questions.stem: At what mean arterial pressure does the lecture start dopamine in cardiogenic shock?
questions.why: A MAP under 60 is where dopamine goes in. Support the pump when the container and the fluid are not the problem.

options.why: Waiting for 40 means waiting far too long.
65 is the general perfusion floor cited elsewhere, not this trigger.
80 is above the threshold given.

questions.stem: You decide early that a patient is septic and then read every later finding as supporting sepsis. Which bias is that?
questions.why: Confirmation bias is selectively weighting evidence that supports the conclusion you already reached. Its close relative, anchoring, is locking onto the first information you received. Both are reasons to re-assess deliberately rather than casually.

options.why: Attribution concerns explaining behavior rather than weighing clinical evidence.
Availability is favoring a diagnosis because a recent case comes to mind.
Anchoring is fixing on the first piece of information; this is the filtering that follows.

questions.stem: How does the review sheet define shock?
questions.why: A state of collapse and failure of the cardiovascular system — body-wide hypoxia from inadequate cardiac output. Cells die, then tissue, then organs, then systems. Without oxygen, cells switch to anaerobic metabolism and lactic acid builds.

options.t: Loss of more than 30 percent of circulating blood volume
options.why: That figure marks decompensation within one type of shock.

options.t: A systolic blood pressure that has fallen below 90 mmHg
options.why: A number is a late sign, not the definition.

options.t: Failure of the respiratory system to oxygenate the blood
options.why: That is respiratory failure, a different problem.

questions.stem: Match the shock category to the part of the perfusion triangle that fails: which shock is a fluid problem?
questions.why: Pump, fluid, container. Cardiogenic fails the pump, hypovolemic the fluid, distributive the container — septic shock through fluid shifts from infection, neurogenic through loss of vascular tone.

options.why: Neurogenic shock is a form of distributive shock, so also a container problem.
Distributive shock is a container problem — the system leaks.
Cardiogenic shock is a pump problem.

questions.stem: Which system does the review sheet call the last resort in compensating for shock?
questions.why: Epinephrine and norepinephrine go first — raising rate, contractility and vascular tone — with baroreceptors driving vasoconstriction and chemoreceptors watching CO2. RAAS is the slower hormonal backstop when those are not enough.

options.why: The sympathetic response comes early, not last.
Baroreceptors activate the vasomotor center early in compensation.
Chemoreceptors monitor CO2 shifts throughout, rather than acting as a last resort.

questions.stem: What does the review sheet name as the number one priority in managing shock?
questions.why: Airway and ventilation first, then high-flow oxygen, then IV fluid to maintain perfusion — not in cardiogenic shock — then treat life threats as they appear. Keep the patient warm, and be off scene in ten minutes or less.

options.t: IV fluid given to raise the blood pressure to normal
options.why: Fluid comes after the airway, and is for perfusion rather than a pressure number.

options.t: Keeping the patient warm throughout the call
options.why: Warmth is on the list but is not the first priority.

options.t: Rapid transport, prioritized above every other action
options.why: Transport matters, but the airway comes first.

questions.why: Once the heart muscle itself becomes ischemic, the pump that would drive any recovery is failing. That is the point past which restoring volume and pressure no longer restores the patient.

options.t: A systolic blood pressure that has fallen below 60 mmHg
options.why: A low pressure is a finding within decompensated shock, not the definition of irreversible.

options.t: Loss of consciousness in a patient who was previously alert
options.why: Altered mental status appears well before shock becomes irreversible.

options.t: Failure of two or more organ systems simultaneously
options.why: Multiple organ failure is the outcome that follows rather than the definition.
